findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting permanently increases reported financing cost ratio by 104 basis points
findings.detail: From 2024/25, IFRS 16 lease accounting is included in financing cost calculations. This raises the financing cost ratio from 8.45% to 9.49% of net revenue stream. This is an ongoing accounting presentation change that affects all future period comparisons and how the council's financial flexibility appears to external stakeholders.
findings.matters: Financing cost ratios are a key metric for lenders assessing borrowing capacity and financial sustainability. A permanent 104 basis point increase in the reported metric will affect lending decisions and covenant assessments, even though this is purely an accounting reclassification rather than a change in actual debt service costs.
findings.figures: 8.45% (excluding IFRS 16), 9.49% (including IFRS 16), effective from 2024/25
findings.quote: Within the operational boundary and authorised limit, allowance was made for debt financing of the planned capital programme, existing financing, PFI liabilities, and anticipated additional lease financing following the adoption of IFRS 16 (Leases) in 2024/25.

findings.headline: Capacity and culture risk: scale of change required outstrips available resources and staff resilience
findings.detail: The paper identifies a new governance focus area on capacity and culture, noting that the scale of change required (financial reform, government reform, possible local government reorganisation, and transformation) creates a risk that the council lacks the capacity and culture to deliver. A prioritisation exercise is planned for September 2026 and staff support for resilience during change is recognised as needed.
findings.matters: If a council's leadership and workforce lack the capacity to execute a turnaround plan, the plan will fail. This signals execution risk on the Finance Improvement Plan and transformation programme, and increased probability that financial targets will not be met.
findings.figures: Transformation programme not yet approved; new capacity and culture improvement area added
findings.quote: Given the scale of change that the Council must deliver in response to Government reforms, and to support the financial challenges, there is a risk regarding the capacity and culture required to deliver the scale of change required.

findings.headline: Internal Audit Opinion is 'reasonable' not 'effective', with four key improvement areas identified
findings.detail: The 2025-26 Internal Audit Opinion states the council's governance, risk management and control framework is 'reasonable' with controls working in practice, but the paper highlights four key areas for further improvement. This is a qualified audit opinion rather than unqualified assurance.
findings.matters: A 'reasonable' audit opinion is less strong than 'effective' and signals that controls are not operating optimally. Four identified improvement areas suggests systemic governance weaknesses that could affect financial control and decision-making.
findings.figures: Four key governance improvement areas identified in section 5.1
findings.quote: The Internal Audit Opinion for 2025/26 is that the Council's framework of governance, risk management and management control is 'reasonable' and that audit testing carried out during the year has demonstrated controls to be working in practice. The assessments contained within this document highlight that there are effective arrangements in place to continue to deliver good governance, but that four key areas are highlighted to further improve our governance.

findings.headline: External auditors (KPMG) have raised significant concerns on financial resilience; s151 Officer has issued formal warning under Local Government Act 2003
findings.detail: The paper references both the KPMG external audit report on financial resilience and a formal statement from the s151 Officer under section 25 of the Local Government Act 2003 (the statutory duty to report if spending commitments cannot be met). Both are cited as core to understanding the council's difficult position.
findings.matters: A section 25 statement is a formal statutory warning that the council may not be able to meet its commitments. This is a direct signal to lenders that the council's finances are at serious risk of not being serviceable.
findings.figures: CIPFA Financial Resilience review referenced; s151 Officer statement appended to Revenue Budget 2026/27
findings.quote: The financial situation of the Council remains extremely difficult, as reflected in the CIPFA Financial Resilience review, the report of our External Auditors (KPMG) and the statement of the s151 Officer pursuant to section 25 Local Government Act 2003

findings.headline: Finance Improvement Plan adoption required to address structural income and expenditure gap
findings.detail: The paper identifies a structural income and expenditure gap requiring delivery of a Finance Improvement Plan, adopted in December 2025. A Finance Improvement Group has been established for external challenge and assurance. The paper emphasises the plan is essential for achieving financial resilience without EFS, but does not provide evidence of full delivery.
findings.matters: A structural gap by definition cannot be closed by efficiency alone; it indicates the council's service scope or funding model must change. Failure to deliver a credible plan means indefinite dependence on exceptional support.
findings.figures: Finance Improvement Plan adopted December 2025; Finance Improvement Group established
findings.quote: It is therefore essential that the Finance Improvement Plan be delivered to address the structural income and expenditure gap in the Council's finances and to achieve financial resilience without the need of EFS.

findings.headline: DSG high needs deficit reduced by £4.8m but statutory override expires March 2028, creating s114 risk
findings.detail: The high needs deficit within the Dedicated Schools Grant was reduced by £4.8m compared to forecast. However, the statutory override that keeps DSG deficits off the general fund expires 31 March 2028. The paper explicitly states the override exists to prevent catastrophic balance-sheet failure and an s114 scenario (formal declaration that spending commitments cannot be met).
findings.matters: Once the override ends in March 2028, DSG deficits will hit the general fund balance sheet directly. Without a credible high-needs funding solution, the council faces a potential s114 notice, the most serious governance failure a council can declare.
findings.figures: £4.8m reduction in DSG high needs deficit compared to forecast outturn; statutory override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The DSG statutory override (which keeps deficits off councils' general fund) remains in place until 31 March 2028. The write-off is intended to ensure that when the override ends, councils are not exposed to catastrophic balance-sheet failure, resulting in a s114 scenario.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support of £17m required for 2025-26 with compound interest repayment obligation
findings.detail: The council has secured exceptional financial support (EFS) funding to mitigate the outturn impact and ensure adequate reserves. EFS was initially forecast at £20m but reduced to £17m following Q3-Q4 improvements. However, EFS is explicitly stated as short-term assistance and must be repaid with compound interest, creating a future debt servicing burden.
findings.matters: EFS debt must be repaid with compound interest, creating a future liability that compounds the structural deficit. Reliance on EFS signals the council cannot balance its budget from revenue, raising questions about the viability of its current service model.
findings.figures: £20m initial requirement, reduced to £17m for 2025-26; £3.2m reduction between Q3 and Q4 outturn
findings.quote: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) funding has again been secured to mitigate the impact of the 2025/26 outturn on the Council's General Fund and to ensure that there are adequate reserves. However, EFS is short-term assistance, it is not a sustainable long-term solution and EFS funding must be repaid with compound interest.

findings.headline: Structural budget overspend of £9.5m with provisional outturn £192.9m against budget of £183.4m
findings.detail: The 2025-26 financial year ended with net expenditure of £192.9m against a net budget of £183.4m, representing an adjusted overspend of £188.8m. Drivers include increased placement costs in adults and children's social care, reduced government funding support, slower tax base growth, and higher capital financing and interest costs on borrowing.
findings.matters: Structural deficits signal underlying spending pressures that cannot be solved through one-off savings; they indicate permanent cost drivers or revenue inadequacy that affects the council's long-term sustainability and ability to service debt.
findings.figures: £192.9m net expenditure, £183.4m net budget, £188.8m adjusted overspend
findings.quote: The provisional outturn position for 2025/26 is £ 192.9 million of net expenditure against a net budget of £ 183.4m, with an adjusted overspend position of £188.8m.

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit & Risk Committee - Treasury Management Review 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's short-term borrowing tactic (12-18 months) now exposed to refinancing risk as PWLB rates have risen and volatility increased
findings.detail: The council deliberately focused on shorter-term loans to maintain flexibility and limit long-term rate exposure. However, it now acknowledges 'increased geopolitical uncertainty and inflationary pressures due to the conflict in the Middle East have heightened interest rate risk' and will review strategy for 2026/27. PWLB 25-year rates rose from 5.8% to 6.2% in one year. Short-term loans represent £74.2m, or 24% of total borrowing, requiring refinancing within one year.
findings.matters: A tactical bet on falling rates is now exposed to refinancing £74m of debt into a higher-rate environment, increasing debt service costs at a time of budget stress
findings.figures: Short-term loans £74.2m (24.36% of £304.7m); PWLB 25-year rate: 5.8% (May 2025) to 6.2% (May 2026)
findings.quote: However, increased geopolitical uncertainty and inflationary pressures due to the conflict in the Middle East have heightened interest rate risk. As a result, the Council will review its treasury management and borrowing strategy for 2026/27 to ensure it remains appropriate in a more volatile interest rate environment.

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit & Risk Committee - Treasury Management Review 2025-26
findings.headline: Directly owned commercial property portfolio generating negative return of -0.26% after financing costs
findings.detail: The council's £33.6m commercial property portfolio delivered rental income of £2.789m but incurred MRP costs of £0.943m and interest costs of £1.533m, resulting in a net loss of £87k. The portfolio is eroding rather than supporting the council's financial position at a time it depends on Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.matters: A loss-making property portfolio reduces financial resilience when the council is dependent on emergency government support and facing depleting reserves
findings.figures: Commercial property holdings £33.6m; Net income less MRP & interest -£87k; Rate of return after financing costs -0.26%
findings.quote: Rate of return, after MRP and interest (Net income less MRP & interest ÷ property valuation) (0.26%)

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit & Risk Committee - Treasury Management Review 2025-26
findings.headline: Liability benchmark projected to exceed capital financing requirement in 2027/28, forcing council to fully deplete internal resources and rely entirely on external borrowing
findings.detail: The council's liability benchmark is projected to exceed its CFR in 2027/28 (£435.4m v £422.3m). The council explicitly states it 'will become increasingly reliant on external borrowing to support both its capital programme and liquidity requirements, thereby exposing it to heightened interest rate and refinancing risks'. Usable reserves declined from £41.7m to £39.3m in one year.
findings.matters: Exhaustion of internal resources means the council will depend entirely on external debt markets for all borrowing with no internal buffer against refinancing risk or interest rate shocks
findings.figures: Liability benchmark 2027/28 £435.4m exceeds CFR £422.3m by £13.1m; Usable reserves down £2.4m year-on-year
findings.quote: The Council will become increasingly reliant on external borrowing to support both its capital programme and liquidity requirements, thereby exposing it to heightened interest rate and refinancing risks.

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit & Risk Committee - Treasury Management Review 2025-26
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support continues and is projected to drive 83% of capital financing requirement growth over next two years
findings.detail: West Berkshire received £16.8m in EFS in 2025/26, continuing support that began in 2024/25. The council projects that over the next two years, only 17% of capital financing requirement growth will come from capital expenditure, with 83% from EFS. This indicates the council is using government emergency support to manage structural budget pressures.
findings.matters: EFS is reserved for councils facing unmanageable financial pressures; its continued use and growth signals credit stress affecting repayment capacity and financial sustainability
findings.figures: £16.8m EFS in 2025/26; EFS projected to account for 83% of CFR increases over 2026-28
findings.quote: Across the next two financial years, approximately 17% of the forecast increase in the CFR relates to capital expenditure, with the remaining 83% attributable to EFS.

findings.paper_title: 4. Financial Statements 2025-26 Highlights and Going Concern Assessment (Friday 17 July 2026)
findings.headline: Trade receivables increased sharply by £4.2m, signalling collection pressure
findings.detail: Year-end trade receivables rose from £7.3m (2024/25) to £11.5m (2025/26), a 58% increase. This appears as part of a broader rise in short-term debtors from £41.3m to £47.6m. This suggests slowing cash collection or service users struggling to pay.
findings.matters: Rising receivables can indicate either delayed collection (a cash-flow pressure) or deteriorating debtor quality. Combined with the council's existing reliance on government support, this suggests cash inflows are tightening.
findings.figures: Trade receivables: £7.3m → £11.5m (increase of £4.2m); short-term debtors: £41.3m → £47.6m
findings.quote: Short-term debtors are above the prior year equivalent, being £47.6m against £41.3m within current assets. The main driver is a £4.2m increase in year-end trade receivables to £11.5m (2024/25: £7.3m).

findings.paper_title: 4. Financial Statements 2025-26 Highlights and Going Concern Assessment (Friday 17 July 2026)
findings.headline: Long-term borrowing increased by £27.8m to £230.5m during the year
findings.detail: The council's long-term PWLB borrowing rose from £202.7m (2024/25) to £230.5m (2025/26). This was deliberate borrowing activity to support capital investment, occurring while the council is already receiving government emergency support for revenue.
findings.matters: Rising debt while dependent on government support and holding minimum reserves suggests the council is stretching its borrowing capacity to fund capital plans. This limits future borrowing headroom and increases fixed debt service costs.
findings.figures: Long-term borrowings: £202.7m → £230.5m (increase of £27.8m)
findings.quote: The growth in long-term borrowings (up from £202.7m to £230.5m) is due to the Council's borrowing activity with the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) increasing during the current financial year.

findings.paper_title: 4. Financial Statements 2025-26 Highlights and Going Concern Assessment (Friday 17 July 2026)
findings.headline: £24.9m Schools' DSG deficit poses a latent threat to General Fund if statutory override ends
findings.detail: The council carries a Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit of £24.9m sheltered by a statutory accounting override extending to 31 March 2028. Management explicitly states: 'Any future removal of the accounting override will constitute a significant financial threat to the Council as the General Fund balance will need to be sufficient to absorb a cumulative deficit balance.' The council is pursuing a High Needs Stability Grant (decision pending from Department for Education) that could reduce this by up to 90%, but this is not secured.
findings.matters: This represents a contingent liability larger than the entire General Fund. If the override is removed and the DfE grant is not awarded, the council would be forced to use reserves to absorb the deficit, likely triggering an emergency situation.
findings.figures: DSG deficit: £24.9m; potential DfE grant could reduce this by up to 90%; override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The Council's DSG Adjustment Account has a deficit balance of £24.9m as at 31 March 2026. Any future removal of the accounting override will constitute a significant financial threat to the Council as the General Fund balance will need to be sufficient to absorb a cumulative deficit balance.

findings.paper_title: 4. Financial Statements 2025-26 Highlights and Going Concern Assessment (Friday 17 July 2026)
findings.headline: General Fund at absolute minimum threshold with no safety margin
findings.detail: The General Fund balance remains at £10.6m, which management confirms is 'at the minimum required threshold of 5% of the net revenue budget requirement for 2026/27'. This leaves no buffer above the statutory minimum for unforeseen pressures or service demands.
findings.matters: A council operating at minimum reserves has zero contingency capacity. Any budget variance or unexpected cost would require immediate draws on earmarked reserves or further government support.
findings.figures: General Fund: £10.6m at 5% minimum threshold
findings.quote: The General Fund remains at the same level as the prior year and at the minimum required threshold of 5% of the net revenue budget requirement for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 4. Financial Statements 2025-26 Highlights and Going Concern Assessment (Friday 17 July 2026)
findings.headline: Net assets declined by £51.2m in a single year
findings.detail: Net assets fell from £280.7m (2024/25) to £229.5m (2025/26). The main driver is a £15.5m increase in the pension liability (from £68.2m to £83.7m), offset partly by improved deficit position. This represents significant erosion of the council's equity base.
findings.matters: Declining net assets indicate shrinking financial buffers. A council with weakening balance sheet position represents higher lending risk, particularly if the trend continues.
findings.figures: Net assets: £280.7m → £229.5m (decrease of £51.2m); Pension liability: £68.2m → £83.7m
findings.quote: The Council's 2025/26 net assets position was £229.5m (2024/25: £280.7m)

findings.paper_title: 4. Financial Statements 2025-26 Highlights and Going Concern Assessment (Friday 17 July 2026)
findings.headline: Council is dependent on government Exceptional Financial Support to fund operations
findings.detail: West Berkshire received £16.8m of government EFS during 2025/26 and has a further £30m earmarked for 2026/27. Management notes this £30m is 'deemed sufficient to support the Council's expenditure plans for 2026/27'. This signals underlying revenue stress that the council cannot meet through its own resources.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether a council can operate independently. Reliance on discretionary government support means the council's financial capacity rests on political decision-making rather than sustainable operations.
findings.figures: £16.8m applied during 2025/26; £30m earmarked for 2026/27
findings.quote: £16.8m was applied during 2025/26. A further £30m of EFS has been earmarked to facilitate the Council's 2026/27 financial commitments.

findings.paper_title: 3a. West Berkshire Council - Initial External Audit Plan 2025-26
findings.headline: Rebuilding assurance work includes detailed reserve reconciliation and balance sheet assessment
findings.detail: KPMG's 2025-26 audit includes targeted rebuild work (£40,000 cost) that specifically reconciles reserve movements across budget-setting and monitoring reports, reviews capital processes, and performs caption-by-caption balance sheet assessment covering the entire disclaimed period.
findings.matters: Reserve adequacy and balance sheet accuracy are core measures of financial sustainability. The targeted focus on these items as part of the rebuild indicates prior audit procedures could not verify them, creating uncertainty about the council's true financial position.
findings.figures: £32,000 risk assessment + £8,000 substantive work for rebuild assurance; materiality threshold £12.6m
findings.quote: Reconciling the planned movement in reserves from budget setting, in year monitoring and outrun reports and documenting our understanding if planned usage and changes in reserves over the disclaimed period. Considering the processes over capital additions/disposals. A balance sheet financial statement caption by caption assessment of the movement over the disclaimed period

findings.paper_title: 3a. West Berkshire Council - Initial External Audit Plan 2025-26
findings.headline: West Berkshire has disclaimed audit opinions for three consecutive financial years
findings.detail: The council's predecessor auditor issued disclaimers for two years through 2022/23. KPMG issued a disclaimer for 2023/24 on 28 February 2025 and another for 2024/25 on 27 February 2026. This means financial statements for these three years have not been audited and carry no audit opinion, indicating the council could not resolve underlying audit issues within statutory deadlines.
findings.matters: Multiple consecutive disclaimed opinions mean the council cannot provide verified financial statements to investors or creditors. This is a fundamental credibility failure that prevents lenders from reliably assessing financial position and viability.
findings.figures: Three consecutive years without audit opinions: 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25
findings.quote: For the Council this had the impact of disclaimers of opinion issued by your predecessor auditor for two financial years up to and including 2022/23. We then issued a disclaimer of opinion for 2023/24 on 28 February 2025 to comply with the statutory backstop date as reported to your previously. For the 2024/25 audit we issued a disclaimer opinion on 27 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: 7. Executive - Financial Performance Report 2025_26 Outturn - Final
findings.headline: Adult Social Care's planned £1.5m divestment of care home properties did not proceed, removing a material revenue saving
findings.detail: The council had planned to divest its own care homes and achieve a £1.5m saving in 2025/26. This divestment 'did not occur', leaving the overspend unreduced. The care homes are now being retained, but the business case or capability to divest was not completed.
findings.matters: Failure to execute a major asset sales plan suggests either weak financial planning, governance issues, or challenges with asset disposals that a lender should understand.
findings.figures: £1.5m unachieved saving, part of £2.1m Own Care Homes overspend
findings.quote: Own Care Homes adverse variance of +£2.1m: Driven by +£1.5m, as the divestment saving target was not achieved due  to the non-divestment of the properties

findings.paper_title: 7. Executive - Financial Performance Report 2025_26 Outturn - Final
findings.headline: £14.3m of capital expenditure slipped into 2026/27 and 2027/28 will now be financed at higher borrowing rates, increasing overall programme cost
findings.detail: The council has reprofiled £14.3m of planned capital spending into future years. Interest rates have risen materially: PWLB 25-year certainty rates increased from c.5.8% in May 2025 to c.6.2% in May 2026. The council states this delayed spending 'is expected to increase the overall cost of delivering the capital programme'.
findings.matters: Delayed capital delivery increases borrowing costs; this is a direct cost consequence of execution delays and will worsen affordability if slippage continues.
findings.figures: £14.3m slipped, PWLB rates 5.8% (May 2025) → 6.2% (May 2026), 40 basis point increase
findings.quote: However, with the cost of borrowing continuing to increase, the reprofiling of £14.3m of capital expenditure into 2026/27 and 2027/28 is expected to increase the overall cost of delivering the capital programme, as this expenditure will be financed at higher rates than originally assum ed. For example, in May 2025, the PWLB 25 -year certainty rate for annuity loans was c. 5.8%. At the start of May 2026, this rate had increased to c. 6.2%.

findings.paper_title: 7. Executive - Financial Performance Report 2025_26 Outturn - Final
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision increased 47% in one year and is forecast to reach £9.2m by 2032/33, creating material future affordability challenges
findings.detail: MRP (the statutory charge for debt repayment) jumped from £4.5m in 2024/25 to £6.6m in 2025/26 and is forecast to reach £9.2m by 2032/33. The council states this 'rising trajectory represents an important consideration in assessing the ongoing affordability of the capital programme'. This reflects the council's shift to annuity-method depreciation on recent capital spending.
findings.matters: Rising MRP is a structural charge on revenue that will constrain future service spending and borrowing capacity; it reflects the cost of past capital decisions now crystallizing.
findings.quote: The MRP charge for 2025/26 was £ 6.6m versus a MRP charge of £4.5m in 2024/25. This is forecast to increase to approximately £9.2m by 2032/33. This rising trajectory represents an important consideration in assessing the ongoing affordability of the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: 7. Executive - Financial Performance Report 2025_26 Outturn - Final
findings.headline: Budgeted savings achieved at only 85%, with £1.6m of planned £10.7m savings not delivered
findings.detail: While the council describes this as 'largely achieved', £1.6m of planned savings did not materialize. The largest gaps were Adult Social Care £1.7m (care home divestment not executed) and Resources £1.1m (transformation work not delivered). This shows gaps in execution capability on financial improvement plans.
findings.matters: A 15% savings shortfall suggests the council cannot reliably deliver planned cost reductions, a material risk for future budget balancing.
findings.figures: £9.1m achieved of £10.7m target (85%), £1.6m shortfall. ASC £1.7m not achieved, Resources £1.1m not achieved
findings.quote: Budgeted savings were largely achieved (Green) in the year with £9.1m/ 85% out of a possible £10.7m Budget Target.

findings.paper_title: 7. Executive - Financial Performance Report 2025_26 Outturn - Final
findings.headline: Social care demand exceeded budget by £6.6m, representing the majority of the adverse variance and driven by uncontrollable volume and rate increases
findings.detail: Adult Social Care overspent by £3.0m (55% of adverse variance) and Children's Social Care by £3.6m (66% of adverse variance). In Children's, residential care placements alone were £3.3m over budget with 5 more children in care than budgeted and average costs per placement 28% above budget. These are ongoing structural pressures, not one-off items.
findings.matters: Social care is statutory and largely demand-led; unbudgeted volume growth of this scale indicates the council's baseline budget assumptions are materially wrong and the problem will recur.
findings.figures: +£3.0m Adult Social Care, +£3.6m Children's Social Care, +£3.3m Placements (£2.4m volume, £0.9m rate), 5 additional children in residential care
findings.quote: The position continues to be driven primarily by social care demand pressures. Further detail on all services is below . To provide context on the scale of the  social care  pressures within the overall Council outturn, +£3.0m/ 55% of the adverse variance relates to Adult Social Care, while +£3.6m/ 66% relates to Children's Social Care.

findings.paper_title: 7. Executive - Financial Performance Report 2025_26 Outturn - Final
findings.headline: Council requires £20m maximum Exceptional Financial Support from MHCLG to balance 2025/26 accounts, indicating structural budget gap
findings.detail: The council's revenue outturn is £5.5m (3.0%) adverse to budget, leaving it unable to balance without government support. MHCLG have provisionally agreed a maximum £20m to apply to reserves to support close of accounts and underpin the 2026/27 budget. The council states this ongoing requirement 'highlights the structural imbalance within the revenue budget between funding statutory obligations and funds available'.
findings.matters: Reliance on exceptional government bailout to meet statutory budget is a red flag for lenders; it indicates the council cannot balance on its own resources.
findings.figures: £20m EFS cap, £5.5m adverse variance (3.0% of £183.4m budget)
findings.quote: MHCLG have provisionally agreed to a maximum of £20m being applied to the Council's reserves to support the 2025/26 close of the accounts and underpin a minimum General Fund requirement to support the 2026/27 revenue budget

findings.paper_title: 6c1. Assets Optimisation Plan - Report for Executive - June 2026
findings.headline: Implementation flagged as urgent with potential serious financial implications if delayed
findings.detail: The decision document explicitly indicates that delays in implementation could have serious financial implications for the council and is marked as urgent. This signals the council views the plan as time-critical to financial recovery.
findings.matters: Urgency suggests the council is under acute time pressure; failure to implement rapidly could result in financial stress and potential breach of borrowing covenants.
findings.figures: No figures provided
findings.quote: Delays in implementation could have serious financial implications for the Council

findings.paper_title: 6c1. Assets Optimisation Plan - Report for Executive - June 2026
findings.headline: Council targeting recurring revenue savings through estate rationalisation
findings.detail: The plan aims to deliver ongoing revenue savings through estate rationalisation, optimisation of income, co-location and reduced running costs. No specific savings targets are disclosed in this report, but these are presented as a core mechanism to stabilise finances.
findings.matters: Revenue savings from asset efficiency are part of the financial recovery plan; their absence or delay would require alternative savings or borrowing.
findings.figures: No specific savings figures disclosed
findings.quote: Deliver ongoing revenue savings through estate rationalisation, optimisation of income, co-location and reduced running costs

findings.paper_title: 6c1. Assets Optimisation Plan - Report for Executive - June 2026
findings.headline: Plan is core to Finance Improvement Plan responding to structural budget challenges
findings.detail: The Assets Optimisation Plan forms a key component of the Finance Improvement Plan approved December 2025. The council explicitly faces structural budget challenges and increasing demand. The plan is designed to stabilise the council's financial position and reduce reliance on reserves.
findings.matters: Structural budget challenges indicate underlying financial unsustainability; this asset plan is the council's response, so its success is critical to financial recovery.
findings.figures: Finance Improvement Plan approved December 2025
findings.quote: The Council faces ongoing financial pressures, including structural budget challenges and increasing demand, and must take proactive steps to stabilise its finances and build resilience.

findings.paper_title: 6c1. Assets Optimisation Plan - Report for Executive - June 2026
findings.headline: Asset disposal programme already in motion delivering £2m+ capital receipts
findings.detail: The council has already approved and is executing asset disposals expected to yield over £2m in capital receipts. If applied to the capital programme, a £2m receipt would reduce borrowing need and avoid financing costs of circa £80k per annum at the council's current weighted average cost of capital of 3.92%.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether asset-backed capital funding is realistic given market conditions and whether £2m is material to the council's overall capital and borrowing plan.
findings.figures: £2m+ anticipated capital receipts; £80k per annum financing costs avoided; 3.92% weighted average cost of capital
findings.quote: These will deliver anticipated capital receipts in excess of £2m.

findings.headline: Collection Fund deficit on Council Tax nearly trebled in one year, from £0.99m to £2.81m, indicating deteriorating collection or tax base.
findings.detail: The Collection Fund deficit on Council Tax is forecast to increase from £0.99m in 2025/26 to £2.81m in 2026/27, a 184% increase in a single year. The paper describes this as 'latest modelling of forecast deficit' and references 'a significant readjustment of the Council Tax base' in the MTFS appendices. This deterioration is outside the council's direct control and reduces reliable revenue further.
findings.matters: Deteriorating collection rates indicate either reduced tax base or payment difficulties in the local community. This reduces predictable funding and creates additional budget pressure.
findings.figures: Collection Fund deficit 2025/26 -£0.99m, 2026/27 -£2.81m, 184% increase
findings.quote: Collection Fund Deficit on Council Tax Latest modelling of forecast deficit -0.99 [2025/26], -2.81 [2026/27]

findings.headline: Schools balances are diminishing and once they decline into deficit, the deficit becomes automatically chargeable to the Council's General Fund, creating unforeseen risk.
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer explicitly identifies 'an un-forecast risk to the Council's General Fund from the schools' balances which have been diminishing over recent years.' Under accounting regulations, when overall schools balances turn negative, they are transferred to the council's General Fund, increasing EFS requirements. Detailed work is underway but 'the level of risk' remains unquantified. The HNB deficit is already £47.67m.
findings.matters: Schools deficits automatically transfer to the council's General Fund, further depleting reserves and increasing EFS requests. This is a quantifiable but currently unmeasured liability threatening financial stability.
findings.figures: £47.67m cumulative HNB deficit in DSG, schools balances 'diminishing over recent years'
findings.quote: There currently is an un-forecast risk to the Council's General Fund from the schools' balances which have been diminishing over recent years. Under accounting regulations, once the overall schools' balances decline into deficit this will become chargeable against the Council's General Fund, increasing any EFS requirement.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support dependency forecast to grow to 100.6% of Capital Financing Requirement movement by 2028/29, exceeding total capital financing growth.
findings.detail: EFS allocation as a percentage of CFR movement grows from 48.5% in 2024/25 to 100.6% in 2028/29. This means by 2028/29, the council's total capital financing growth cannot be funded from revenue and will exceed the annual EFS allocation. The Section 151 Officer notes EFS 'comes with a significant cost in the form of MRP' and creates 'longer term financing implications'.
findings.matters: When EFS exceeds 100% of CFR movement, the council cannot fund even ordinary capital replacement from revenue. This signals structural unsustainability and indefinite dependency on EFS support.

findings.headline: In 2027/28, the Liability Benchmark exceeds the Loans CFR, indicating the council has exhausted internal resources and faces full exposure to interest rate risk.
findings.detail: Treasury forecasts show the Liability Benchmark (£435.4m in 2027/28) exceeding the Loans CFR (£422.3m), indicating negative investable resources. The Section 151 Officer explains this means 'the Authority has depleted all internal resources and is fully exposed to interest rate and refinancing risks for the full CFR.' It requires 'long term borrowing to fund capital and liquidity' with 'rare' occurrence indicating 'immediate need' for external borrowing.
findings.matters: This is an extreme financial position indicating the council must borrow for liquidity. It creates severe interest rate and refinancing risk and signals potential inability to fund capital programmes or manage emergencies.
findings.figures: 2027/28 Liability Benchmark £435.4m vs Loans CFR £422.3m, Closing CFR 2028/29 £475.3m
findings.quote: If the benchmark is higher than external loans (loans CFR), it signals an immediate need to take on long term borrowing to fund capital and liquidity, as essentially the Authority has depleted all internal resources and is fully exposed to interest rate and refinancing risks.

findings.headline: Capital financing costs forecast to exceed the council's 10% fiscal rule threshold, reaching 12.1% of net revenue stream in 2027/28.
findings.detail: Capital financing requirement is £18.9m in 2026/27 (11% of net revenue stream) and forecast to reach 12.1% in 2027/28, breaching the council's own fiscal rule. This is driven by Minimum Revenue Provision costs on Exceptional Financial Support and High Needs Block deficit financing. The Section 151 Officer states 'significant adjustment to spending plans in 2026/27 would be required' to prevent financial distress indicators.
findings.matters: Capital financing exceeding 12% of revenue stream leaves less money for service delivery. Exceeding fiscal rules signals financial distress and unsustainability of the current path.
findings.figures: £18.9m capital financing 2026/27, 11% of net revenue stream 2026/27, 12.1% forecast 2027/28, 10% fiscal rule threshold
findings.quote: For 2026/27, the actual percentage is 11% and more than the historic fiscal rule.

findings.headline: Retained Business Rates income halved from £30.57m to £13.27m in a single year, a 57% reduction in a major funding stream.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 funding settlement shows retained business rates collapsing from £30.57m in 2025/26 to £13.27m in 2026/27. This structural reduction is unrelated to collection issues and represents a permanent reduction in the council's funding base. Overall Core Spending Power decreased 2.5% compared to 2025/26, with no offsetting increase in other income sources.
findings.matters: A 57% reduction in a major funding stream cannot be managed through modest savings. This structural underfunding indicates the council cannot balance its budget without ongoing EFS or further service reductions.
findings.figures: £30.57 million retained business rates 2025/26, £13.27 million 2026/27, 57% reduction
findings.quote: Retained Business Rates Government prescribed under settlement: 30.57 [2025/26], 13.27 [2026/27]

findings.headline: Adults and Children's social care commissioning budgets show net growth of £11.67m in 2026/27 with savings of only £3.32m against pressures of £14.99m.
findings.detail: The budget paper identifies £9.22m modelled Adult Social Care pressures and £5.78m Children's Social Care pressures (total £14.99m) but proposes only £2.37m and £0.95m in savings respectively (total £3.32m). The Section 151 Officer acknowledges this is demand-led with poor historical delivery: 'Ambitious and challenging savings strategies have been identified in recent years, however, in some instances due to marketplace factors, savings have been undeliverable.'
findings.matters: Uncontrollable demand-led cost growth indicates structural budget pressure. If the council cannot deliver planned social care savings (as proven by recent history), further budget deficits and EFS requests will follow.
findings.figures: £14.99m total social care pressures 2026/27, £3.32m savings identified, £9.22m adult pressures, £5.78m children's pressures
findings.quote: Modelled Adult Social Care Pressures 9.22, Modelled Adult Social Care Savings -2.37, Modelled Children's Social Care Pressures 5.78, Modelled Children's Social Care Savings -0.95, Net Social care Pressures 11.67

findings.headline: £4.25m of previously planned savings have been removed from base budget because they were unachievable due to marketplace factors and inflationary pressures.
findings.detail: Historic savings totalling £4.25m are being realigned out of the base budget, including £1.48m from care home outsourcing, £1.00m transformation savings, £0.47m resource centre externalisation, and £0.41m from development and regulation fee income. The Section 151 Officer explicitly notes 'in some instances due to marketplace factors, savings have been undeliverable' and that recent 'savings strategies have been identified' but are eroded by costs like national living wage rises.
findings.matters: Failure to deliver £4.25m of planned savings indicates the council's budget forecasting is unreliable. If this scale of savings could not be achieved, confidence in new proposed savings targets should be questioned.
findings.figures: £4.25m total budget realignments, £1.48m care homes externalisation, £1.00m transformation, £0.47m resource centres, £0.41m fee income
findings.quote: Transformation savings 1.00, Care Homes - externalisation of service 1.48, Externalisation of Resource Centres 0.47, Development & Regulation - unachiveable fee income 0.41

findings.headline: General Fund reserve of £10.6m is being eroded by in-year overspends and is forecast to fall well below the Section 151 Officer's recommended 5% minimum.
findings.detail: The council's General Fund reserve of £10.6m as of 31st March 2025 is under pressure from significant in-year overspends against Adults and Children's Social Care commissioning budgets in 2025/26. The Section 151 Officer states the available reserve will be 'well below the s151 recommended 5% of net revenue budget'. The 2026/27 budget plans to draw down a further £2.82m from reserves to fund the budget gap.
findings.matters: Reserves below minimum thresholds indicate financial vulnerability and increase the risk of a Section 114 notice. Low reserves limit the council's ability to absorb unexpected cost variations or emergencies.
findings.figures: £10.6 million General Fund 31 March 2025, £2.82 million planned drawdown 2026/27, 5% recommended minimum
findings.quote: The Council's reserve position is delicate, with the existing General Fund (£10.6 million as of 31st March 2025), generated from Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), under pressure from in-year overspends (2025/26).

findings.headline: High Needs Block deficit forecast to reach £47.67m by March 2027, increasing by £16.98m in 2026/27 alone, held on the balance sheet as unusable reserves.
findings.detail: The cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block deficit held on the council's Balance Sheet under statutory accounting override will be £47.67m by March 2027, up from £30.68m at March 2026. This £16.98m increase in 2026/27 is driven by increased demand for independent and non-maintained special school placements and rising Educational Health Care Plans in mainstream schools.
findings.matters: The HNB deficit constrains the council's usable resources and capital financing capacity. It directly impacts borrowing capacity, reserve adequacy, and the council's ability to manage unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: £47.67m cumulative deficit at March 2027, £30.68m at March 2026, £16.98m increase in 2026/27
findings.quote: the forecast cumulative deficit as at 31st of March 2027 is £47.67m

findings.headline: Council is dependent on £30m Exceptional Financial Support from central government to set a balanced budget; without it, would be in a Section 114 position.
findings.detail: The net revenue budget requirement is £210.9m against available funding of £178.1m, creating a £32.82m funding gap. This is proposed to be funded through £2.82m of reserves and a £30m EFS request submitted on 12th December 2025. The Section 151 Officer states the decision 'remains outstanding at the time of writing this report' and without EFS approval, the council would face insolvency.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can set a balanced budget without external government support. A Section 114 notice means the council cannot spend money and may need to cease services.
findings.figures: £210.9 million net revenue budget requirement, £178.11 million funding available, £32.82 million funding gap, £30 million EFS request
findings.quote: Without EFS, the Council, as with many other upper tier authorities will be in a Section 114 position given the absence of significant and robustly substantiated savings programmes.

findings.headline: Previously planned savings have been found unachievable or eroded by inflation; outsourced services (care homes) and efficiency targets no longer viable
findings.detail: Savings that were assumed in prior-year budget plans have been rebased or removed entirely after review. Market factors prevented achievement of outsourcing targets (care homes, resources centres), and staff efficiency gains were eroded by national living wage rises and employer NI contribution increases. This represents loss of anticipated budget headroom and signals that future savings targets may face similar obstacles.
findings.matters: Inability to deliver planned efficiency savings raises questions about feasibility of the £15m annual savings targets assumed for 2027/28 onwards; it suggests the council's cost base is becoming rigid and unresponsive to efficiency action
findings.figures: Unquantified individually but represents material rebasing of the budget base for 2026/27
findings.quote: For financial year 2026/27, a number of historic savings, some of which upon review have been deemed to be unachievable due to either market place factors (the outsourcing of care homes and resources centres, increases in planning income), or eroded due to escalating inflationary pressures (staff efficiencies, eroded through national living wage rises, employer NI contribution changes), have been rebased or removed from the base budget.

findings.headline: Council will have no internal investable resources left from 2027/28 onwards; Liability Benchmark exceeds CFR and council becomes fully exposed to interest rate risk
findings.detail: The council's reserves and cash balances will be fully depleted by 2027/28 when the Liability Benchmark exceeds the Capital Financing Requirement. From that point, all borrowing will be at market rates with no buffer from internal resources. Simultaneously, capital financing costs are projected to grow £14.8m over the MTFS (from £15.6m to £30.92m), driven by EFS financing and rising interest costs.
findings.matters: Total depletion of reserves removes financial flexibility and crisis buffers; full exposure to interest rate movements creates unhedgeable risk; rising financing costs as a percentage of revenue (8.5% to 15.9% of net revenue stream) signals unsustainable debt trajectory
findings.figures: 2027/28 Liability Benchmark £435.4m vs CFR £428.6m; capital financing costs grow from £15.6m (2025/26) to £30.92m (2029/30); financing costs as % of revenue stream rises from 8.5% (2025/26) to 15.9% (2029/30)
findings.quote: Based on current projections in the MTFS, and the EFS requirement to support the reserves and net revenue budget in 2026/27, the Liability Benchmark will exceed the CFR in financial year 2027/28. This effectively means the internal investable resources (reserves, cash balances), have been fully depleted from an internal financing perspective and the Authority is fully exposed to interest rate risk.

findings.headline: Council tax base reduced by 854 dwellings and collection rate cut from 99.5% to 98.6%, creating permanent £12.5m revenue loss
findings.detail: The council has revised down its tax base assumptions after reviewing actual dwelling numbers and collection patterns. Slower housebuilding (attributed to sustained high interest rates) and increased demand for council tax support and reliefs have combined to reduce the tax base. This adjustment permanently reduces the council's own-resource funding capacity and reduces settlement-based CSP growth from £19.8m to £14.9m.
findings.matters: A shrinking tax base signals local economic difficulty and reduces the council's borrowing capacity (which is often based on tax base multiples); it indicates a structural, not cyclical, revenue weakness
findings.figures: Reduction of 854 equivalent dwellings; collection rate reduced from 99.5% to 98.6%; cumulative revenue reduction £12.5m over MTFS period; reduces CSP growth from £19.8m to £14.9m
findings.quote: The Council's collection rate, historically set at +99%, has been adjusted to 98.60%. The number of taxable dwelling has been reduced by 854. The reduction in growth compared to projections is largely attributable to the wider economic environment, with the building of anticipated developments slowing in a prolonged period of high interest rates. The cost-of-living crisis has also resulted in the number of households seeking support and reliefs to grow during the reporting period.

findings.headline: Adult and children's social care commissioning costs are the dominant expenditure driver, projected to grow £39.4m (net) over the MTFS as unit costs continue rising sharply
findings.detail: Social care is described as the primary driver of the £53.3m net revenue budget growth. Unit costs are escalating due to both complexity of need and market factors (national living wage, employer NI). The top 25 individual care packages alone cost £13.1m in 2025/26 compared to £4.9m in 2019/20 — a 168% cost inflation in four years. The council requires £33.7m net investment in commissioning budgets across the MTFS.
findings.matters: Social care is demand-led and largely fixed in the short term; rising unit costs show no signs of stabilisation; this expenditure pressure is outpacing all other council services and cannot be easily controlled through efficiency savings
findings.figures: Social care commissioning growth +£39.4m net; top 25 care packages £13.1m (2025/26) vs £4.9m (2019/20); £33.7m net investment required over MTFS
findings.quote: This growth (excluding savings targets), in expenditure primarily relates to social care commissioning budgets +£39.4 million and growth in the base budget +£41.2 million, driven by annual pay inflation, pension deficit contributions, and contractual inflation on supplies & services contracts. In financial year 2025/26, the total annual cost of care packages for the top twenty-five packages amounted to £13.1 million, compared to £4.9 million in 2019/20.

findings.headline: Central government EFS requests escalating from £20m (2025/26, revised upward) to £47m annually by 2028/29, totalling £184m over five years
findings.detail: The 2025/26 EFS request was revised sharply upward from £3m provisional to £20m as the in-year financial position deteriorated. Thereafter annual requirements climb steeply: £30m (2026/27), £40m (2027/28), £47m (2028/29-2029/30). By 2028/29, EFS accounts for over 100% of the council's capital financing requirement movement, meaning the entire borrowing need is being funded by revenue capitalisation.
findings.matters: Escalating EFS requests signal that structural budget pressures are worsening rather than stabilising; EFS is unsustainable medium-term and dependent on continued government forbearance; it also drives up Minimum Revenue Provision costs in future years
findings.quote: However, a challenging 2025/26 in year financial position, has presented a significant pressure against the Council's minimal General Fund, resulting in a revised 2025/26 £20 million EFS request as detailed below... The Council is in receipt of financial support from Central Government (2024/25 £13 million, and 2025/26 provisionally agreed £3 million, with revised request for £20 million submitted).

findings.headline: Council cannot balance 2026/27 budget without further central government support; faces Section 114 notice if denied
findings.detail: After completing savings identification exercises, the council explicitly states it cannot set a balanced 2026/27 budget without additional EFS. The s151 officer is required to issue a Section 114 notice if this support is not approved or alternative major efficiencies are not presented. This pattern repeats annually throughout the MTFS period.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal statement of financial distress that triggers statutory intervention; it signals the council cannot meet its statutory duty to balance the budget and represents a material governance failure
findings.quote: Following the conclusion of savings identification exercises, the Council is unable to set a balanced budget for financial year 2026/27 without seeking additional financial support from Central Government. A request for such financial support was submitted on 12th December 2025. Without approval of this support, or alternatively a robust plan of efficiencies (of such scale, well beyond those of prior financial years), provided for review to the Executive, the s151 officer will be required to issue a Section 114 report/notice. This pattern is repeated annually throughout the MTFS.

findings.headline: Capital programme is 53% funded by external grants, creating delivery risk if funding does not materialise.
findings.detail: Of the £171m four-year programme, only £49.2m (29%) comes from council funding. The largest source is grants and contributions (£91m, 53%), with S106 and CIL making up the remainder (£30.9m, 18%). If grant funding does not materialise as planned, the programme cannot proceed as specified.
findings.matters: Lenders assess execution risk; heavy dependence on external grant funding creates a material risk that planned projects do not proceed on schedule or at all.
findings.quote: Council Funding: 49,210,177; Grants & Contributions: 90,966,446; S106: 8,888,650; CIL: 21,996,958; Total Planned Expenditure: 171,062,231

findings.headline: Development in Lambourn catchment is currently stalled and the council is investing £2.1m to unlock it.
findings.detail: The Nutrient Neutrality project (2026-27: £2.1m) is explicitly described as addressing a constraint where development is 'currently stalled due to the anticipated impact of additional nutrients and phosphates on the Lambourn catchment'. This signals growth prospects in the area are constrained by environmental regulation and the council sees removal of this constraint as a priority investment.
findings.matters: Development constraints directly affect the council's ability to grow its tax base and economic activity; this shows material headroom to unlock.
findings.quote: This will unlock development which is currently stalled due to the anticipated impact of additional nutrients and phosphates on the Lambourn catchment.

findings.headline: SEND School programme contains £12m in a single year (2029-30), signalling material increase in demand for special education provision.
findings.detail: The Special Education Needs & Disabilities School programme totals £13.6m across four years, with negligible spending in years 1-3 but £12m concentrated entirely in 2029-30. The description notes this is 'to fulfil the requirement for a strategic response to increase sufficiency to address increasing demand'. This timing suggests the council has identified a material, accelerating need for SEND places.
findings.matters: A significant future commitment to a growing cost area; a lender needs to assess whether the council can absorb this spike, and a S151 needs to plan reserve and funding strategy around it.
findings.quote: To fulfil the requirement for a strategic response to increase sufficiency to address increasing demand for tailored, cost-effective SEND provision (Special Education Needs & Disabilities)

findings.headline: Capital financing costs exceed the 10% revenue limit from 2027/28 and continue rising
findings.detail: The ratio of capital financing costs to net revenue stream breaches the council's adopted 10% maximum in 2027/28 (reaching 12.1%) and continues rising to 15.9% by 2029/30. This means debt servicing is consuming an ever-larger share of available revenue.
findings.matters: Unsustainable financing ratios reduce capacity for service investment and indicate deteriorating financial sustainability as debt costs dominate budget flexibility.
findings.quote: The adopted ratio above, although compliant in 2026/27, is exceeded in 2027/28

findings.headline: Council moves into negative working capital from 2025/26, driven by borrowing and High Needs Block deficit
findings.detail: Working capital (current assets minus current liabilities) turns negative from 2025/26 onwards, indicating the council owes more in the short term than it has in liquid resources. This is driven by increasing borrowing liabilities and growing High Needs Block deficits.
findings.matters: Negative working capital signals potential liquidity stress and suggests difficulty managing short-term obligations without further borrowing or asset sales.
findings.quote: From 2025/26 the Authority moves to a negative working capital position, this is primarily driven by increasing current liabilities relating to borrowing, and revenue pressures alongside the increasing High Needs Block deficit

findings.headline: General Fund reserves collapse from £15.83m to £0.52m over four years
findings.detail: The General Fund falls from £15.83m in 2025/26 to £12.17m (2026/27), £8.02m (2027/28), and just £0.52m by 2028/29—essentially zero. This eliminates the council's ability to absorb unforeseen costs or variations in income.
findings.matters: Minimal reserves mean the council cannot manage volatility in demand, inflation, or income without service reductions or further borrowing.
findings.quote: the Authority's investable resources are being depleted over the life of the MTFS, with usable reserves (even after application of EFS), are reducing

findings.headline: Internal reserves will be fully exhausted by 2027/28, forcing full exposure to interest rate risk
findings.detail: The Liability Benchmark will exceed the Capital Financing Requirement in 2027/28, meaning the council will have depleted all internal cash resources. Once reserves are gone, the council must borrow for all future needs and has no buffer against interest rate movements.
findings.matters: Complete depletion of internal resources eliminates financial flexibility and forces the council into perpetual external borrowing with no shock absorption capacity.
findings.quote: the Liability Benchmark will exceed the CFR in financial year 2027/28. This effectively means the internal investable resources (reserves, cash balances), have been fully depleted from an internal financing perspective and the Authority is fully exposed to interest rate risk

findings.headline: Council's own treasury assessment concludes it is experiencing 'financial distress'
findings.detail: The council's finance team explicitly describes its position as showing 'a level of financial distress', with future financing driven by EFS requests rather than capital programmes. This language from management signals awareness of structural problems beyond cyclical pressures.
findings.matters: When a council's own finance officers describe the position as financially distressed, it indicates serious creditworthiness concerns and reduced repayment capacity.
findings.figures: Financing costs as % of net revenue: 10.0% (2026/27), 12.1% (2027/28), 14.3% (2028/29), vs 10% adopted maximum
findings.quote: The financing ratio, alongside the liability benchmark demonstrates a level of financial distress, with treasury indicators highlighting financing requirements in financial years, subsequent to 2026/27, being heavily influenced by EFS requests as opposed to purely financing historic and proposed capital programmes

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) becomes the primary driver of borrowing need, not capital spending
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing requirement (CFR) is increasingly driven by capitalisation of revenue overspends rather than actual capital investment. EFS requests are rising from £30m in 2026/27 to £47m by 2028/29, and by 2028/29, 100% of CFR growth will be EFS-driven. This indicates the council cannot balance its revenue budget without government support.
findings.matters: Dependence on discretionary EFS rather than self-sufficiency signals structural budget imbalance and reliance on government support that may not continue indefinitely.
findings.quote: by the end of the MTFS, 100% of the movement in CFR will be driven by EFS

findings.headline: MTFS projects a significant funding gap in 2026/27, with revenue capital financing requirements as a contributing factor
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy shows a material funding gap in the coming financial year. The gap is partly driven by revenue capital financing costs (debt servicing for the capital strategy), indicating that revenue pressures and capital financing costs are both squeezing the budget.
findings.matters: A funding gap signals the council must make additional savings, raise income, or draw down reserves; gaps that persist suggest structural deficit
findings.figures: Funding gap amount not specified but described as 'significant'
findings.quote: The proposed MTFS details a significant funding gap for financial year 2026/27. An element of the gap is being driven by the revenue capital financing requirement (debt servicing), incurred supporting delivery of the Council's Capital Strategy and the associated programme of works.

findings.headline: PWLB borrowing rates at 5.5% against historic 2-3% average, significantly raising financing costs
findings.detail: High interest rates substantially increase the cost of capital financing, compressing the revenue budget further and reducing the affordability of the capital programme. This is a key constraint on the council's ability to deliver investment.
findings.matters: Higher debt servicing costs reduce available revenue for services and capital investment; further rate rises would worsen the funding gap
findings.figures: 5.5% current PWLB rates vs historic 2-3% average
findings.quote: The Council's ability to deliver a capital programme has been constrained by two key factors: Firstly, by a high-interest rate environment, Public Works and Loan Board (PWLB) rates on average being around 5.5% compared to a historic 2 -3% average.

findings.headline: Council-funded capital programme significantly reduced; shift to external grants as internal resources are depleted
findings.detail: Capital investment capacity is being squeezed as EFS requirements and HNB deficit consume Balance Sheet resources. The council is actively refocusing the capital programme onto only key projects and moving toward reliance on external grants and contributions rather than council borrowing.
findings.matters: Reduced capital investment signals constraints on infrastructure maintenance and service improvement; long-term asset condition and service delivery may deteriorate
findings.figures: £49 million council-funded capital vs £165 million EFS need over MTFS
findings.quote: The Council-funded (i.e. debt funded) capital programme over the life of the MTFS (2026/27 -2029/30) has been significantly reduced compared to prior financial years. The reduction has been driven by a significant increase in the Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR), through an increasing need to seek Exceptional Financial Support (EFS).

findings.headline: High Needs Block deficit growing from £30.5m to £51.7m, eroding usable reserves and forcing external borrowing
findings.detail: The DSG-related HNB deficit is forecast to grow substantially and is being held in unusable reserves under statutory override until 31 March 2028. This is reducing working capital and forcing the council to borrow externally to support both capital and capitalised revenue expenditure.
findings.matters: A structural overspend in education demand is forcing external borrowing; the statutory override ends in 2028, at which point the deficit could impact the General Fund directly
findings.figures: £30.5 million by 31st March 2026, increasing to an estimated £51.7 million by 31st March 2027
findings.quote: The HNB deficit (related to the DSG), which is currently subject to a statutory override, (i.e. the deficit is held within the Council's Balance Sheet in unusable reserves as opposed to impacting the Council's General Fund), is forecast to be in the region of £30.5 million by 31st March 2026, increasing to an estimated £51.7 million by 31st March 2027.

findings.headline: Council forecasts over £165 million in Exceptional Financial Support needs over the MTFS period
findings.detail: EFS represents capitalised revenue overspends that must be financed through Minimum Revenue Provision charges back to the revenue budget. Against this, the council plans only £49 million in council-funded capital expenditure, meaning revenue account problems are consuming capital financing capacity.
findings.matters: EFS is a symptom of structural revenue deficit; it signals financial distress and requires government intervention, while consuming revenue that would otherwise fund services or investment
findings.figures: over £165million EFS need vs £49million planned council-funded capital expenditure
findings.quote: During the life of the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS), there is a current projected need for EFS of over £165million compared to planned Council-funded capital expenditure of £49million.

news_drafts.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting permanently increases reported financing cost ratio by 104 basis points
news_drafts.lead: Financing cost ratios are a key metric for lenders assessing borrowing capacity and financial sustainability. A permanent 104 basis point increase in the reported metric will affect lending decisions and covenant assessments, even though this is purely an…

news_drafts.headline: Capacity and culture risk: scale of change required outstrips available resources and staff resilience
news_drafts.lead: If a council's leadership and workforce lack the capacity to execute a turnaround plan, the plan will fail. This signals execution risk on the Finance Improvement Plan and transformation programme, and increased probability that financial targets will not…

news_drafts.headline: Internal Audit Opinion is 'reasonable' not 'effective', with four key improvement areas identified
news_drafts.lead: A 'reasonable' audit opinion is less strong than 'effective' and signals that controls are not operating optimally. Four identified improvement areas suggests systemic governance weaknesses that could affect financial control and decision-making.
